page.title: Pick the right front door: Front Door, Application Gateway and Traffic Manager
page.lede: Walk the decision tree, follow a shopper in Surabaya to the nearest edge and a healthy origin, watch a web application firewall block a SQL-injection request, and see Traffic Manager fail over through DNS. Press ▶ Play, or step through with Next and Back.
page.svgTitle: Choosing and combining Azure Front Door, Application Gateway, Traffic Manager and Load Balancer
page.svgDesc: A decision tree asks whether traffic is HTTP or HTTPS and whether it spans regions. A shopper in Surabaya reaches the Jakarta edge of Front Door, which forwards to a healthy origin and switches to Southeast Asia when Indonesia Central fails. Inside a region, an Application Gateway routes by path to two App Service apps and its web application firewall blocks a SQL-injection request with 403. Finally, Traffic Manager answers DNS lookups for a point-of-sale service and fails over to priority 2 once the cached answer expires.

steps.title: Which service goes in front?
steps.text: Nusantara Retail's storefront needs three things at once: send /images/* to a new images app, stop attacks such as SQL injection before they reach the code, and keep selling if a whole region fails. Azure has four services that can stand in front of an application. Two questions pick the right one — and sometimes the answer is two services working together.

steps.title: Question 1: is it HTTP or HTTPS?
steps.text: Application Gateway and Front Door are reverse proxies: they end the connection, read each HTTP request, and can route it by host name or path, end TLS and run a web application firewall. That is built for web traffic. For anything else — a point-of-sale sync over plain TCP, a game over UDP — you need layer 4 or DNS: Load Balancer or Traffic Manager.

steps.title: Question 2: one region or several?
steps.text: Inside one region, Application Gateway handles web traffic and Azure Load Balancer everything else. Across regions you need a global service. Front Door is a global proxy that runs in Microsoft's edge locations. For other protocols, the cross-region load balancer offers one static anycast IP, while Traffic Manager steers clients with DNS answers — any protocol, but its failover waits for DNS caches.

steps.title: Nusantara's answer: two services
steps.text: The storefront is web traffic for shoppers all over Indonesia, with a standby region. So Front Door works at the edge, in front of an Application Gateway in each region that routes paths to the apps. The stores' point-of-sale sync is plain TCP between two regions, so it gets a Traffic Manager priority profile. Now follow a shopper in Surabaya through this design.

steps.title: A shopper in Surabaya reaches the nearest edge
steps.text: A shopper in Surabaya opens the storefront on her phone. Front Door's DNS and network send her to a nearby edge location — Jakarta — instead of a server far away. TLS ends at the edge and the WAF policy checks her request there. Product photos are cached at the edge too, so a repeat request for an image never leaves Jakarta.

steps.title: A healthy origin answers
steps.text: Prices and stock can't come from a cache, so the edge forwards the product page over Microsoft's network to an origin. The origin group lists two Application Gateways: Indonesia Central with priority 1 and Southeast Asia with priority 2. Health probes run all the time, and both answer. Front Door picks the healthy origins with the best priority, then the lowest latency.

steps.title: Origin 1 fails: the edge switches
steps.text: Indonesia Central stops answering its health probes, so the edge stops sending requests there and forwards them to Southeast Asia, which serves the catalogue in browse-only mode. The shopper notices little: she still talks to the same Jakarta edge, so no DNS answer has to change and no cache has to expire. When Indonesia Central recovers, priority 1 takes the traffic back.

steps.title: Inside a region: the host name trap
steps.text: Zoom into one region. The Application Gateway's listener accepts the request, and its rule picks an App Service app. But App Service finds an app by its host name, and the gateway's default probe asks for 127.0.0.1. Neither app recognises that name, so both probes fail. With no healthy backend, the shopper gets 502 Bad Gateway.

steps.title: Fix the host name, then route by path
steps.text: Two settings fix it: the backend settings pick the host name from the backend target, and a custom probe takes its host name from those settings. Both apps turn healthy. Now the rule's path map does its job: /images/* goes to the images app and everything else to the storefront app — one address, two apps, each receiving its own name.

steps.title: The WAF blocks SQL injection
steps.text: An attacker sends ?id=1' OR 1=1-- hoping the database returns every customer. The WAF policy, now in Prevention mode, checks the request against Microsoft's Default Rule Set. The SQL-injection rule is critical and adds 5 points; at a total of 5 the request is blocked. The attacker gets 403 Forbidden, and the storefront never sees the request. Shoppers carry on as normal.

steps.title: Traffic Manager answers with DNS
steps.text: The stores' point-of-sale sync uses plain TCP, so it gets Traffic Manager. A terminal in Makassar looks up the service's name. Its DNS resolver asks Traffic Manager, which returns the healthy endpoint with the best priority: Indonesia Central. The resolver may cache that answer for the 30-second TTL. The terminal then connects to the endpoint directly; Traffic Manager never sees the traffic.

steps.title: Priority 1 fails, the answer changes
steps.text: Indonesia Central stops responding. Traffic Manager's health probes fail several times in a row, the endpoint turns Degraded, and from now on Traffic Manager answers with Southeast Asia, priority 2. But this terminal's resolver still holds the old answer, so the terminal keeps trying the failed region until the cached answer expires. DNS failover is only as fast as the caches allow.

steps.title: After the TTL, the terminal follows
steps.text: Thirty seconds later the cached answer expires. The next lookup reaches Traffic Manager, which now returns Southeast Asia, and the terminal reconnects there. Total failover time is roughly detection time plus the TTL plus any extra caching by the client. A lower TTL fails over faster but multiplies DNS queries. When Indonesia Central recovers, new answers move back to priority 1.

steps.title: Recap: global in front, regional behind
steps.text: Two questions — HTTP or not, one region or several — pick the service. Front Door handles the global edge, caching and fast origin failover. Application Gateway routes by path inside a region and carries the WAF policy. Traffic Manager steers any protocol with DNS but waits for caches, and the cross-region load balancer gives TCP and UDP one anycast address.
